thread: Mercy that humiliates: a kindness can wound the person who receives it, and the debt it creates may be harder to bear than the need
summary: Each piece asks what it costs to be the one who is helped. Nietzsche argues it: the pitying person, he says, wounds the pride of the sufferer and leaves a debt that breeds resentment, so the better kindness is the one that does not announce itself. Kipling images it in a ballad where a soldier who beat and mocked his water-carrier owes him his life, and can only say what that debt is after the man has died. Hugo dramatises it: a convict is forgiven so completely and so publicly that the narrator cannot say whether he is touched or humiliated, and the next chapter shows the cost. Dolly Parton sings around it: a child proud of a gift made with love meets the contempt of other children, and the song is her answer to pity.

pieces.essay: Nietzsche argues it: to see someone suffering and help them is to expose their shame, and great obligations breed revenge rather than gratitude.
pieces.poem: Kipling images it: the man who has been kicked for years is the one who carries the narrator through, and the debt is paid only in an admission.
pieces.story: Hugo dramatises it: the Bishop's generosity leaves Valjean with nothing to push against, and the man has to leave the town as if fleeing it.
pieces.song: Dolly Parton sings around it: the coat is a gift made out of love and poverty, and the song refuses the pity the other children offer.

forYou: For When Jasmine Blooms: a colonial household in 1950s Malaya runs on kindnesses that have to be accepted with thanks, and Hugo and Kipling show two ways a gift can wound the one who takes it.
